kapak.alt: Degree, age at onset and family

youtube.baslik: Language Development in Children with Hearing Loss | Lesson 78 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
How does hearing loss affect a child's language development? In this lesson we look at the effect of the degree of loss and the age at onset, the difference between prelingual and postlingual loss, vocabulary and grammar development, and the role of family involvement and device use.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Moeller (2000), Early intervention and language development in children who are deaf and hard of hearing, Pediatrics; Tomblin et al. (2015), Outcomes of Children with Hearing Loss study, Ear and Hearing supplement; Joint Committee on Infant Hearing, Year 2019 Position Statement; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Degree, age at onset, vocabulary and family
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how hearing loss affects a child's language development.
We will cover the degree of loss, the age at onset, the difference between prelingual and postlingual loss, and the role of the family.
Language outcomes in children with hearing loss vary over a very wide range; no single factor explains this difference.
The first factor is the degree of loss, that is, how much of speech can reach the child.
The second is the age at which the loss began: did it start before or after language was acquired?
The third is how early identification and intervention began.
The fourth is how well the device makes speech audible and how many hours a day it is worn.
The fifth is how involved the family is in the child's language development.
Finally, a significant share of children with hearing loss also have additional developmental needs that can affect language.

notlar.metin: _Harder_ at a distance and in noise

cumleler: The area of the audiogram where everyday speech sounds fall is called the speech banana.
Vowels and consonants such as m and n are strong and lie mostly in the low frequencies.
In this example, we see a loss between thirty and fifty five decibels, in the mild to moderate range.
This child hears that someone is talking but may miss some weak, high-frequency consonants such as s, sh and f.
So the family thinks the child hears, while the child receives words in an incomplete and unclear form.
When the speaker moves away or the room is noisy, even more details are missed.
With mild loss, the child hears speech but misses soft and distant sounds; the effect shows in the fine details of language.
With moderate loss, most speech is heard faintly without a device; vocabulary and grammar development may be affected.
With moderately severe loss, speech is heard only up close and in part; an unaided child is expected to show a clear language delay.
With severe loss, speech is hardly heard at all without a device; an appropriate device is essential for spoken language to develop.
With profound loss, a cochlear implant is considered if there is not enough benefit from hearing aids.
Still, even with the same degree of loss, outcomes differ widely due to factors such as age at intervention and device use.

maddeler.metin: Language built _without full access_ to sound

cumleler: Prelingual hearing loss is loss that is present at birth or begins in the first years, before language is acquired.
These children must build language without enough access to sound; their auditory experience is limited.
So the timing of identification and intervention is one of the strongest factors determining language outcomes.
Postlingual hearing loss begins after the basic structures of language have formed.
These children largely keep their vocabulary and grammar, and usually adapt quickly to sound from an implant or hearing aid.
However, in a child who cannot hear their own voice, the clarity and voice quality of speech may decline over time.
Between these two extremes are losses that begin or progress while language is still developing; these need close monitoring.
Hearing loss can affect not just one area of language but many connected areas.
The area noticed most often and earliest is vocabulary.
Grammar, that is, learning word endings and sentence structures, may also be delayed.
In producing speech sounds, errors may appear, especially for high-frequency consonants that are not heard well.
Social language skills such as joining conversations, taking turns and catching subtle meanings may also be affected.
Since reading and writing are built on spoken language, a weak language foundation also shows in literacy during school years.
Children do not learn words only from what is said directly to them.
A large share of words is picked up by overhearing conversations around them, which is called incidental learning.
A child with hearing loss often cannot hear distant, background or noisy conversations.
So they miss many words that their normal-hearing peers learn on their own.
Since vocabulary is also the basis for learning new words, the gap may grow over time.
For this reason, language development, especially vocabulary, should be measured at regular intervals.
Turkish is an agglutinative language; plural, possession, tense and person are carried by suffixes added to the word.

cumleler.yazi: Some of these suffixes contain high-frequency consonants such as s and ş; for example, the sı in kapısı, his door.
cumleler.ses: Some of these suffixes contain high-frequency consonants such as s and sh; for example, the possessive ending in the Turkish word for his door.

cumleler: A child with high-frequency loss may hear these small pieces of sound incompletely or unclearly.
A child who cannot hear the suffix also misses the grammatical information that changes the meaning of the word.
So making high frequencies audible is especially important for language development when fitting devices.

cumleler.yazi: One of the key studies showing the importance of family involvement is by Moeller, published in Pediatrics in two thousand.

cumleler: In this study, children who began intervention in the first year of life had better vocabulary and verbal reasoning scores at age five.
Family involvement stood out as one of the strongest factors determining language outcomes.
The scores of children who started early and had high family involvement came close to the range of their normal-hearing peers.
Family involvement means talking a lot with the child, reading books, describing daily tasks and taking part regularly in the program.
So early intervention follows a family-centered approach that aims to empower the family as well as the child.
When choosing their child's communication approach, families encounter different options.
Auditory-verbal approaches aim at listening and speaking skills, using the hearing provided by a hearing aid or implant.
Some approaches use hearing together with lipreading, gestures and visual cues.
Sign language, in Türkiye Turkish Sign Language, is a full language with its own grammar and gives access through vision.
In a bilingual approach, the child learns both sign language and spoken language.
Each approach has its own advantages; the choice belongs to the informed family.
The audiologist's task is to give the family unbiased information and to provide the best hearing support, whichever path is chosen.

yan.metin: Better audibility and *longer* use, better language

cumleler.yazi: A large study following children with mild to severe loss is the Outcomes of Children with Hearing Loss, or OCHL, study.
cumleler.ses: A large study following children with mild to severe loss is the Outcomes of Children with Hearing Loss, or O.C.H.L., study.

cumleler: In this study, children whose devices made more of speech audible had better language outcomes.
Children who wore their devices for more hours a day also showed more progress in language development.
So the fitting should be verified with real-ear measurement on the ear and should match the targets.
A well-fitted device worn all day is the most concrete audiological contribution to language development.
We can sum up all these findings as a road: the first step is early identification.
The second step is a suitable hearing aid or implant, with its fitting verified by measurement.
The third step is wearing the device whenever the child is awake.
The fourth step is a rich language environment provided by the family every day.
The last step is regular monitoring of hearing and language development, so that any area falling behind is noticed early.

sahneler.metin: When assessing language, note the hearing age as well as the chronological age. The difference between them helps interpret the rate of progress.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: do not compare a child who started hearing late through an implant or hearing aid only by chronological age.
The time since the child began receiving regular sound is called hearing age.
For example, a child implanted at age three has a hearing age of one year, one year after the implant.
The goal is for the child's language to show at least one year of progress each year and to come closer to peers over time.
If progress is slower than expected, review the device fitting, wearing time and any additional needs.
As the degree of loss rises, access to speech drops; even a mild loss can make a child miss fine details of language.
In prelingual loss, the timing of identification and intervention is among the strongest factors in language outcomes.
Vocabulary and grammatical structures such as suffixes are the areas most often affected.
Early intervention, family involvement and all-day device use clearly improve language outcomes.

sahneler.soru: When does prelingual hearing loss begin?
sahneler.aciklama: Prelingual loss is present at birth or begins _before language is acquired_; the child must build language without full access to sound.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: when does prelingual hearing loss begin?

cumleler: The correct answer is A: before language is acquired.
This loss is present at birth or begins in the first years, so early identification and intervention shape the language outcome.
